headline: Billy's Law gives the Justice Department formal authority to run NamUs, a national database for missing persons and unidentified remains, and requires police to send missing child reports there too.
what_it_does: The law sets the Justice Department's authority to keep the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NamUs) running as it already does. It requires law enforcement agencies that send missing child reports to the FBI's NCIC database to also send those reports to NamUs. It also gives the National Institute of Justice access to NCIC missing and unidentified person records so the two systems can check and match data, and it directs the Justice Department to study the systems and plan for automatic record transfers. Finally, it requires the department to share best practices with forensic medicine providers and police, and to report to Congress every two years on the two databases.

who_it_affects.how: Agencies that report missing children to NCIC must now also submit those same reports to NamUs.

who_it_affects.group: Families of missing children and missing persons
who_it_affects.how: Their cases are now required to be entered into NamUs as well as NCIC, which may make them easier to match with unidentified remains.

who_it_affects.group: Medical examiners, coroners, and other forensic medicine providers
who_it_affects.how: They will receive Justice Department guidance on collecting, reporting, and analyzing data about missing persons and unidentified human remains.
